I would like to prove something by contradiction. Namely, my current goal is s ∩ t = ∅. I can then use

    by_contra h
    rw [← ne_eq] at h

to transform h : s ∩ t ≠ ∅, and I would like to use h to pick an element, via

    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h

however, this does not work, as h is actually h : s ∩ t = ∅ → False and not h : s ∩ t ≠ ∅, as the info view is suggesting. how do i obtain and use the actual proposition that comes from by_contra?
(by_contra! will push the "not" operator into the hypothesis and simplify some obvious equivalence, such as "not eq empty" -> "Set.Nonempty")
It does, I guess the issue was I needed to convert s \neq \empty to s.Nonempty via Set.nonempty_iff_ne_empty first

Right -- s ∩ t ≠ ∅ means s ∩ t = ∅ → False in Lean so I don't know what you mean by "the actual proposition" -- you have got the actual proposition! Formal mathematics is very formal, and takes some getting used to :-)
My personal experience with goals of that sort and what kind of situations they arose from, tells me you may be interested in Set.disjoint_iff_forall_ne. :man_mage: :crystal_ball:
more immediately related to your question is Set.nonempty_iff_ne_empty

Anyway, the issue is here:
incertia said:

h : s ∩ t ≠ ∅, and I would like to use h to pick an element, via

    obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h

however, this does not work

As you discovered, obtain is "dumb" (or "focused"). There's no reason why you'd be able to use obtain with an inequality like that, just like you couldn't use it with h : 2 ≠ 3. The hypothesis you need for obtain is one that says "there exists an element in the set", which is indeed just one lemma away from the inequality

I guess logically speaking, s ∩ t ≠ ∅ says "not forall not", (more precisely, "not (for all x, x is not in s intersect t)" and then you need some statement of logic which translates this into "exists" but the proof of this is not "it's true by definition", the proof is "it's true by some relatively simple logical contortion".
s ∩ t = ∅ also isn't by definition the same as ∀ x, x ∉ s ∩ t, the theorem that they're equivalent uses docs#Set.ext (two sets with the same elements are equal)
